articleTitle: The ALPHET project: A new approach to improve the lifing methodology for thermocouple probes used in gas turbines
publicationTitle: EVI-GTI Conference on Gas Turbine Instrumentation (GTI 2017)
abstract: During ALPHET, a research project funded by Innovate UK, the University of Cambridge and Esterline Advanced Sensors have been collaborating to develop an advanced approach to predict the life of thermocouple probes used in gas turbines. The new methodology combines accelerated laboratory tests based on the salt deposition method with information obtained from other sources, including combustor rig tests, metallurgical analysis of probes returned after engine service and temperature data acquired throughout the long term operation of sensors installed in aero gas turbines. In addition to life assessment of current thermocouple probes, the work includes assessment of advanced materials and the improved lifing methodology can be valuable in indicating the life of future thermocouple sensors that will work at temperatures higher than today's probes. This paper will outline the basis of the methodology and describe the several challenges to be overcome when using complex engineering data obtained from engines.

articleTitle: Automated wireless propagation measurement system for evaluating the deployment of wireless sensor networks in gas turbine engines
publicationTitle: EVI-GTI Conference on Gas Turbine Instrumentation (GTI 2017)
abstract: During their development phase, gas turbine engines may be instrumented with up to 3000 sensors hardwired to a central data acquisition unit by over 12 km of cabling. The use of wireless sensor network (WSN) technologies should lead to reductions in cabling costs and installation time, greater flexibility in sensor deployment, and new methods for onengine sensing. However, reliably and consistently delivering these advantages requires a detailed understanding of the wireless propagation conditions between sensors and the data acquisition `base station' in what is a challenging electromagnetic environment. This paper reports on a fully automated system that utilises software defined radio (SDR) techniques to measure and evaluate the wireless propagation characteristics of this challenging on-engine environment. Using this system, high integrity WSNs may be designed and experimentally evaluated with a level of fidelity that cannot be achieved with existing commercial-off-the-shelf wireless systems. The system has been used to perform wireless propagation measurements on a static Rolls-Royce Trent 900 engine, and to investigate the use of a WSN for replacing some of the hardwired sensors on a development engine. Through the analysis of measurements performed over 7,500 individual wireless channels, the engine RF propagation environment was characterised and the performance of a variety of standards-based and custom wireless transmission techniques were critically evaluated and compared. This research has enabled the delivery of design information required for the development of a prototype on-engine wireless sensor demonstrator.

articleTitle: EMPRESS: A pan-European project to enhance process efficiency through improved temperature measurement
publicationTitle: EVI-GTI Conference on Gas Turbine Instrumentation (GTI 2017)
abstract: The ground-breaking results of a European project called EMPRESS, funded by the EURAMET's European Metrology Programme for Innovation and Research (EMPIR) are described. This three-year project, led by the UK's National Physical Laboratory, started in May 2015, and is intended to significantly enhance the efficiency of high value manufacturing processes by improving temperature measurement capability and implementing traceability to the SI unit of temperature, the kelvin, in-process. Key developments, demonstrated in process, include new ultrastable thermocouples, surface temperature measurement based on phosphor thermometry, and a portable `standard flame' for traceable combustion thermometry.

articleTitle: Applying hardware in the loop to designing, integrating, verifying and validating the control system of new aircraft engines
publicationTitle: EVI-GTI Conference on Gas Turbine Instrumentation (GTI 2017)
abstract: A new experimental rig is presented, developed to design, integrate, verify and validate the control system of the all-new advanced turboprop engine, produced by GE Aviation and chosen by Textron Aviation to power its new Cessna Denali airplane. The ATP Wet Rig has been conceived to demonstrate the successful integration of engine components, to perform a functional verification at software and system level and to allow an early validation of the final engine system in a controlled and safe environment, preliminary to flight test activities. A dedicated Engine Simulator has been developed to run the ATP Engine model within a Hard Real Time framework. It provides aircraft's interfaces emulation, controls the load actuators and the electrical motors' speeds, replicates consistent loads on the components in compliance with the engine simulated status, intercepts all the EECU electrical I/O lines through appropriate “break out boxes” and physical test points, required for integration purposes. Finally, a dedicated Rig Control System has been developed to communicate and to control all the equipment present in the Wet Rig. It is a distributed system responsible for supervision, test point management, data acquisition, subsystems control, safety and equipment management, communication with the Engine Simulator.

articleTitle: Modeling of Pt8W alloy high temperature strain gauge for drift behavior prediction
publicationTitle: EVI-GTI Conference on Gas Turbine Instrumentation (GTI 2017)
abstract: Besides NiCr alloy, Pt8W alloy is one of the most commonly used grids for high temperature strain gauge application. Tungsten in the grid begins to oxidize at a grid temperature > 500-550°C. Due to that, the properties of gauge will change. In this paper, a two layer modeling method is proposed, by which both resistance and gauge factor characteristics up to 700°C can be reconstructed by only measuring room temperature gauge resistance. Furthermore, using an available tungsten oxidation reaction formula, drift behavior under different temperature and oxygen concentrations of the surrounding atmosphere can be estimated. By applying the knowledge from the model, strain measurement uncertainty due to the property change of gauge at alternating temperature can be limited within 2% in ABB turbocharger turbine blade vibration measurement conditions.
